name: Alcohol and antibiotics: what the NHS says
headline: Can you drink alcohol with antibiotics? What the NHS says, and which ones differ
summary: It depends on the antibiotic: the NHS says moderate drinking is unlikely to cause problems with common ones, but firm warnings exist for a few.
keyPoints: The NHS says moderate drinking is unlikely to cause problems with the most common antibiotics, though alcohol may worsen side effects such as nausea or dizziness.
The NHS says to avoid alcohol completely with metronidazole and tinidazole, and NHS 111 Wales names linezolid and doxycycline as interacting with alcohol too.
The NHS says amoxicillin can be taken with alcohol, and that azithromycin can too unless it causes dizziness, although some NHS azithromycin pages are more cautious.
UK sources word the advice differently, so the leaflet in the pack and a pharmacist or GP are the places the NHS points to for a specific antibiotic.
For a serious allergic reaction to an antibiotic, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about drinking alcohol with antibiotics?
body.body:
The NHS says that drinking alcohol in moderation is unlikely to cause problems with the most common antibiotics. It adds that some antibiotics can cause side effects such as feeling sick or dizzy, and alcohol may make these worse. So the answer depends on which antibiotic has been prescribed.

Antibiotics are medicines that treat infections caused by bacteria. The NHS interactions page also points people with doubts towards a GP or pharmacist. Alcohol is only one of the things that page covers, because it also deals with how antibiotics can change the way other medicines and herbal supplements work.

body.heading: Which antibiotics have a specific alcohol warning?
body.body:
A small number of antibiotics carry a firmer warning about alcohol. The NHS says to avoid alcohol completely with metronidazole and with tinidazole. NHS 111 Wales also names linezolid and doxycycline as antibiotics that interact with alcohol.

For linezolid, it suggests avoiding drinks made by fermenting, such as wine, beer, sherry and lager. For doxycycline, it says alcohol can affect how well the medicine works. The NHS page of common questions about doxycycline is reported to say that it is best not to drink alcohol with this medicine, because alcohol can stop it working properly. These are the antibiotics named in the NHS pages retrieved for this guide, not a complete list.

body.heading: What can happen if alcohol is mixed with metronidazole or tinidazole?
body.body:
The NHS says that mixing alcohol with metronidazole can cause nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, hot flushes and a fast, pounding heartbeat. The NHS says this advice applies to metronidazole tablets, liquid and suppositories, and its guidance for the vaginal gel is similar. NHS 111 Wales lists similar effects for metronidazole and tinidazole, including headaches, dizziness and drowsiness.

The NHS says the advice to avoid alcohol carries on for a while after the last dose, which gives the medicine time to leave the body. NHS 111 Wales gives a longer wait for tinidazole than for metronidazole. Other NHS pages give different lengths of time, so the leaflet or the pharmacist can say which applies.

Apart from alcohol, the NHS says there is no need to avoid other food or drink with metronidazole.

body.heading: Why might alcohol matter for side effects and recovery?
body.body:
Some antibiotics cause nausea or dizziness, and the NHS says alcohol can make these feelings worse. For azithromycin, the NHS says that if the medicine makes a person dizzy, alcohol will make them feel worse. The NHS interactions page also says that avoiding alcohol while unwell is generally advised.

The NHS pages retrieved here focus on side effects and specific interactions rather than on how fast the body recovers. For that reason this guide does not claim that alcohol slows recovery from infection.

body.heading: What do the NHS pages say about amoxicillin and azithromycin?
body.body:
Amoxicillin belongs to the penicillin family of antibiotics, and azithromycin to the macrolide family. The NHS common questions page for amoxicillin says alcohol can be drunk while taking it. The same page says no food or drink needs to be avoided with amoxicillin.

For azithromycin, the NHS common questions page says alcohol can be drunk, but not if the medicine causes dizziness. Two other NHS azithromycin pages, About azithromycin and Side effects of azithromycin, word this more cautiously and say alcohol may make a person feel worse. The NHS pages for flucloxacillin, another penicillin, and for ciprofloxacin also say alcohol can be drunk, and the clarithromycin page repeats the caution about dizziness. The wording therefore differs between pages for the same medicine, and a pharmacist can say how it applies to a particular prescription.

body.heading: Do all UK health sources give the same advice?
body.body:
They do not always match. NHS inform, the Scottish NHS information service, says alcohol should not be drunk while taking antibiotics, or for a period after finishing them. NHS 111 Wales gives the same message about moderate drinking as the NHS interactions page, then lists the antibiotics with firmer warnings. An NHS hospital trust leaflet says there are no known interactions between most antibiotics and alcohol, while naming a few exceptions.

This is why the NHS pages keep returning to the leaflet in the pack and to a pharmacist or GP for the antibiotic in question.

body.heading: Who can give advice, and when is it urgent?
body.body:
For a question about one antibiotic and alcohol, the NHS points to a pharmacist or GP. NHS guidance on antibiotic side effects says most are mild, but serious allergic reactions need an emergency response. NHS 111 is the route for urgent advice that cannot wait for a pharmacy or GP appointment.

In rare cases an antibiotic can cause anaphylaxis, a severe and potentially life-threatening allergic reaction. For milder allergic-type reactions that do not improve, the NHS suggests contacting a GP. The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for signs such as a skin rash, wheezing, tightness in the chest or throat, trouble breathing or talking, or swelling of the mouth, face, lips, tongue or throat.
